accept.reason: Timely need: SWE-Bench Verified is near saturation (>70% reported), so a harder issue-resolution benchmark with large headroom (best 23.3% Pass@1) restores signal for agent research.

Contamination-mitigation design that is new for SWE benchmarks: copyleft (GPL) repositories for the public/held-out sets plus purchased private startup codebases, with three access tiers (public, held-out, commercial).
Tasks are substantially larger than SWE-Bench Verified: trivial edits excluded, reference patches average 107.4 LOC across 4.1 files, every task at least 10 changed lines.
accept.location: §1 ("107.4 lines of code across 4.1 files"); Figure 3 caption

accept.reason: Scale and spread: 1,865 problems from 41 repositories (11+12+18), four languages, per-repository cap of 100 instances to limit single-repo overfitting.

Human augmentation adds a problem statement, test-grounded requirements and an explicit interface, removing a known false-negative mode (wrong class/function names) and under-specification of commit-derived tasks.
Test reliability controls: tests run 3 times and flaky ones dropped; annotators filter fail2pass tests that are too broad or irrelevant; problems dropped when no valid test remains.
accept.location: §3.2 Tests ("we run each set of tests 3 times"); §4.3

accept.reason: Public set (731 instances) released; containerized per-language environments; one scaffold (SWE-Agent), one prompt, 200-turn cap, model versions dated; judge prompt given in full.
Evaluates a broad model set under one scaffold: frontier closed models, open-weight models and a SWE-trajectory fine-tuned model (SWE-Smith-32B), on both public and commercial sets.

Diagnostic analyses beyond a single number: per-language and per-repository resolve rates and an LLM-judge failure taxonomy contrasting frontier (semantic/wrong solution) and small models (syntax, tool use, context).
A private held-out set from separate repositories is kept to detect future overfitting to the public set.
Limitations are stated honestly: language coverage, issue-resolution scope only, dependence on tests, and over-prescriptive augmentation.
Task format is concrete and easy to follow, with a full worked example of problem statement, requirements and interface, and a before/after rewrite.
The commercial set gives enterprise codebases no public benchmark has, and the paper reports results on it (best 17.8%).

reject.reason: Table 3 counts are inconsistent with the evaluated set: per-model failure counts exceed both N=731 and the number of unresolved instances, so the unit of the failure analysis is unclear and its percentages cannot be interpreted.
reject.location: Table 3; §6.2 "we programmatically filter to only unresolved instances". Recomputed: Opus 681+239=920, Gemini 491+424=915, GPT-4o 569+220=789, Qwen 386+406=792 > 731; expected unresolved for Opus 731x(1-0.227)=565.
reject.fix: State the unit (runs x instances?), recompute Table 3 on unresolved public instances only; hours.

reject.reason: Results text contradicts Table 1: Sonnet 4 given as 16.3% (Table 1: 17.6) and GPT-4o as 3.9% (Table 1: 4.9).
reject.location: §5 Results "also achieves a 16.3% resolve rate"; "at 3.4% and 3.9% respectively" vs Table 1. Cross-referenced.
reject.fix: Correct the text; minutes.

reject.reason: The commercial set cannot satisfy the stated per-repository range: 276 problems over 18 repositories is about 15 per repository, against 'between 50 and 100 instances' per repository and 'a similar number of problems per repo'.
reject.location: §1 "Each repository contributes between 50 and 100 instances, with a strict cap of 100 instances"; §3.3 (276 problems), Abstract (18 repositories). Recomputed 276/18=15.3.
reject.fix: Report per-repository counts for every subset and restrict the claim to the public/held-out sets; hours.

reject.reason: The headline 'contamination-resistant' claim is argued, not measured: no memorization probe, no public vs held-out comparison (the held-out set exists), and the GPL 'legal barrier' argument is asserted without evidence that copyleft code is absent from training corpora.
reject.location: §3.1 "the nature of these licenses creates legal barriers to their inclusion in commercial training corpora"; Abstract "contamination-resistant testbed"; no contamination experiment in §5-§6 (text search).
reject.fix: Report public vs held-out resolve rates for 2-3 models, add a memorization/completion probe on public repos (e.g., in the style of Golchin & Surdeanu 2024); about one GPU-week plus API cost.

reject.reason: Evaluating closed API models on the private commercial and held-out sets sends that code to model providers; the paper does not discuss how this affects long-term contamination resistance or the data-use terms agreed with the startups.
reject.location: §5 (closed models evaluated on commercial set, Table 2); §3.3; no discussion found.
reject.fix: Describe API data-retention settings and the agreements; a paragraph.

reject.reason: The 'substantially more challenging' comparison is not like-for-like: the >70% figure on SWE-Bench Verified comes from other reports and tuned scaffolds, while SWE-Bench Pro numbers use SWE-Agent with a basic prompt and 200 turns; the same harness is never run on Verified.
reject.location: §1 "substantially lower than the >70% Pass@1 reported on SWE-Bench Verified [15]"; Figure 2 caption; §5. Text search: no Verified run.
reject.fix: Run the same SWE-Agent configuration on SWE-Bench Verified for the Table 1 models; one to two days of API compute.

reject.reason: Single run, no variance or confidence intervals; with N=731 the 95% interval is about ±3.1 pp, so GPT-5 vs Opus 4.1 (23.3 vs 22.7) and the commercial ranking (17.8 vs 14.9, ±4.5 pp at N=276) are not separable, yet the abstract states a ranking.
reject.location: Table 1; Table 2; Abstract "GPT-5 achieving the highest score to date at 23.3%". Binomial SE recomputed.
reject.fix: Report 3 runs or bootstrap CIs; soften ranking language; one to three API-days.

reject.reason: Harness parity and settings are under-specified: open-weight models use 'syntax parsing' for tools while closed models use native tool calls; GPT-5 fails to submit on 63.1% of failures, 97.6% of them tool-use, which suggests a harness incompatibility; temperature, reasoning effort, context limits and cost caps are not stated.
reject.location: §5 "for open-weight models, we use syntax parsing to enable tool-use"; Table 3 GPT-5 row; §6.2 "GPT-5 indicates potential differences in effective-tool-use".
reject.fix: Report all decoding/agent settings; diagnose GPT-5 non-submissions; rerun with a fixed tool interface; days.

reject.reason: The 'long-horizon', 'hours to days' framing is not operationalized: no human solve-time is measured, and the evaluated setting supplies requirements and interfaces that name files, functions and expected strings, turning much of the search into specified implementation.
reject.location: Abstract "may require hours to days for a professional software engineer to complete"; §5 Issue Ambiguity; App. A.2-A.3. Text search: no time measurement.
reject.fix: Measure expert solve time on a sample, or retitle/reframe; report task-length statistics (median LOC, files); weeks for a time study.

reject.reason: No ablation of the augmentation: models are never evaluated without requirements and/or interface, so how much of the task the augmentation gives away, and how hard the underlying issues are, is unknown.
reject.location: §3.1 "the setting without requirements is potentially interesting"; §5 Issue Ambiguity (only the fully specified setting).
reject.fix: Evaluate 2-3 models with statement-only and statement+requirements; one to two API-days.

reject.reason: The human pipeline is undocumented: no annotator count, qualifications, time per task, agreement, QA protocol, or funnel counts (candidate commit pairs to final tasks) for the 'three-stage' process.
reject.location: §1 "We design a novel three-stage human-in-the-loop process"; §4.2-§4.3. Text search: no annotator statistics.
reject.fix: Add a datasheet-style section with funnel counts, annotator details and agreement; a few days of writing.

reject.reason: Resolvability is asserted but not validated: no human solves a sample, and no failed model patches are audited for false negatives, although tests are acknowledged as an imperfect verifier.
reject.location: Abstract "All tasks are human-verified and augmented with sufficient context to ensure resolvability."; §7.1 Dependency on Test Suite.
reject.fix: Have engineers solve a random sample from the statement+requirements alone; audit ~100 failed patches; one to two weeks.

reject.reason: Figure 1 states 'difficulty filtering', but the text describes only a size filter; if tasks were filtered by model success, the low resolve rates are partly by construction.
reject.location: Figure 1 caption "We design the dataset with contamination resistance, difficulty filtering, and human augmentation/verification."; §4.
reject.fix: State every filter, and whether any model was used to select tasks; minutes.

reject.reason: The failure-mode analysis has weak validity: GPT-5 judges its own trajectories, only the last 20 turns are read, the human agreement behind the 20-turn choice is not reported (the 87% figure is borrowed from [22]), the prompt's 10 categories do not map stated onto Table 3's 9 columns, 'Other' is 63.4% of Sonnet's submitted failures, and the prompt hard-codes 'Final state: Failed (no successful patch generated)' even for submitted patches.
reject.location: §6.2 "utilizing GPT-5 as the judge", "We determined 20 turns to have the highest correspondence with human validations"; Table 3; App. B.1.
reject.fix: Report human agreement on a labelled sample, use a judge not under evaluation (or several), give the category mapping; days.

reject.reason: Analysis text misreads Table 3: Qwen's tool-use share is 349/792=44.1%, not 42.0%, and it is not the highest (GPT-5: 446/724=61.6%).
reject.location: §6.2 "exhibits the highest tool error rate (42.0%)"; Table 3 Qwen and GPT-5 rows. Recomputed.
reject.fix: Correct the sentence; minutes.

reject.reason: The delta over prior SWE benchmarks is a refinement: the commit-pair sourcing, fail2pass/pass2pass tests and human verification follow SWE-bench/SWE-Bench Verified; contamination-resistant and multi-language SWE benchmarks (SWE-bench-Live [25], Multi-SWE-bench [24], SWE-rebench, SWE-Lancer, LiveCodeBench) are not compared, and 'the first to systematically apply such a methodology' is not supported.
reject.location: §1 "to the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to systematically apply such a methodology"; §2.1 (no comparison table); §4.1. Literature check offline: memory, [verify].
reject.fix: Add a comparison table vs prior SWE benchmarks (size, languages, LOC, contamination strategy) and narrow the 'first' claim; a day.

reject.reason: The public-commercial gap is attributed to enterprise complexity without controls: the commercial set has no reported statistics (Figure 3 covers the public set only), languages or task sizes may differ, and Table 2 omits two Table 1 models.
reject.location: §1 "underscoring the greater complexity of enterprise codebases"; §5; Table 2 vs Table 1; Figure 3 caption.
reject.fix: Report commercial-set statistics and a size/language-matched comparison; a day.

reject.reason: The held-out set is undescribed: no statistics or results, so 'mirroring the public set' cannot be checked.
reject.location: §3.3 "We hold out a set of 858 problems mirroring the public set but use a separate set of repositories."
reject.fix: Report summary statistics and one model's score; hours.

reject.reason: Language coverage is narrow (Python, JS, TS, Go), weaker than prior multi-language SWE benchmarks, which limits the 'diverse' claim.
reject.location: §7.1 Limited Language Coverage; §2.1 Multi-SWE-bench covers seven languages.
reject.fix: Narrow the diversity wording or add languages; months for new data.

reject.reason: Commercial results cannot be reproduced by others by design; environments 'will be released'; agent configuration files are not given.
reject.location: §3.2 "All environments will be released as pre-built docker images"; §3.3 Commercial.
reject.fix: Release images and configs; offer a hosted evaluation for the commercial set.

reject.reason: Citation errors: SWE-Bench is cited as [25] (SWE-bench goes live!) in the abstract; 'social media posts [1, 25]' cites two arXiv papers; SWE-Bench Verified is cited as [13] (original SWE-bench); SWE-Smith is evaluated but not cited.
reject.location: Abstract "builds upon the best practices of SWE-Bench [25]"; §1 "social media posts [1, 25]"; §1 "SWE-Bench Verified [13]"; §5 SWE-Smith; References. Cross-referenced.
reject.fix: Fix the references; minutes.

reject.reason: Presentation is thin for a main-track paper: short analysis, typos ("models current perform better"), inconsistent names ("DeepSeek Qwen-3 32B", 'private set' for held-out), Figure 4 caption refers to file/LOC bins it does not describe, and Table 3 columns are not defined.
reject.location: Figure 4 caption; §5 "earlier generation models like DeepSeek Qwen-3 32B"; §5 "we keep the private set held-out"; Table 3.
reject.fix: Copy-edit; define columns; a day.

reject.reason: Data-governance details are missing: terms under which startup code was purchased and may be evaluated, contributor consent, annotator compensation, GPL compliance for the redistributed public set.
reject.location: §3.1 "where we contacted the company and purchased their engineering repos"; §4.1. Text search: no ethics statement.
reject.fix: Add an ethics/data statement; hours.

reject.reason: Anonymization: the text names the organization whose employees founded some source startups, which identifies the authors in a double-blind venue. Flagged for the editor; not a scientific weakness.
reject.location: §4.1 "startups founded by Scale employees"
reject.fix: Remove identifying text; minutes.

reject.reason: Only the mean patch size is given; with a 10-line minimum and only 'over 100 tasks' above 100 lines, the distribution is heavy-tailed and the median would say how many tasks are actually large.
reject.location: §1 "Every problem involves at least 10 lines of change, and over 100 tasks demand more than 100 lines of modification."; "107.4 lines"
reject.fix: Report median and quartiles of LOC and files per subset; minutes.

reject.reason: Agentless is dismissed as producing 'low evaluation scores' without numbers, so scaffold sensitivity of the benchmark is not shown.
reject.location: §5 Scaffold "Agentless has difficulty in multi-file editing, thus, produces low evaluation scores"
reject.fix: Report the Agentless numbers; hours.

reject.reason: No date-based contamination check: commit dates of public and commercial tasks are not reported against model training cutoffs, so even a simple temporal check of the contamination claim is impossible.
reject.location: §4.1 (commit-pair sourcing, no dates); §5 "latest versions as of September 18th, 2025". Text search: no commit dates.
reject.fix: Report commit-date distributions and resolve rate before/after each model's cutoff; hours.

reject.reason: Description of the requirements contradicts the example: §4.2 and A.2 say requirements do not prescribe implementation or leak solutions, yet the A.2 example fixes file paths, a function name and a tuple's contents.
reject.location: §4.2 "does not prescribe how the solution should be implemented"; App. A.2 "Requirements never include specific code implementation and don’t leak solutions." vs A.2 example (`stage_from_google_books`, `STAGED_SOURCES`).
reject.fix: Describe precisely what requirements may specify; quantify leakage via R10; hours.
